name: Valles Marineris
description: One of the most prominent features on the surface of Mars, Valles Marineris is a gigantic gash in the planet’s crust. It is a system of gigantic canyons that stretch well over 4,000 km (2,485 miles), from Noctis Labyrinthus in the west to the chaotic terrain above the outflow channels into the Chryse Basin to the east. It dwarfs the Earth’s Grand Canyon; if Valles Marineris were placed in the United States, it would stretch all the way between the east and west coasts. From the southern rim of Melas Chasma to the northern rim of Ophir Chasma measures nearly 600 km (373 miles) across, and has depths reaching about 7 km (4.4 miles). The origin of Valles Marineris is still not fully understood, but it was almost certainly not formed by flowing water, as were typical (though much smaller) canyons on Earth. Rather, it probably was the result of tectonic faulting, possibly related to the massive Tharsis volcanic region to the northwest. Though not originally formed by water, flowing water may have played a role in altering the terrain in many parts of this region.
caption: View of Vallis Marineris, colored using elevation data - white is high elevation, purple is low elevation.

name: Tharsis Volcanic Region
description: Tharsis is a gigantic volcanic plateau that is home to some of the solar system’s largest volcanoes. These include Arsia Mons, Pavonis Mons, and Ascraeus Mons. Arsia Mons is 435 km (270 miles) in diameter, has a summit 17.7 km (11 miles) high, and a summit caldera about 110 km (68 miles) across. Pavonis Mons is 380 km (236 miles) in diameter, has a summit 14 km (8.7 miles) high, and a summit caldera 91 km (57 miles) across. Ascraeus Mons is 480 km (298 miles) in diameter, but extensive lava aprons extend for a total width of about 870 km (540 miles). Its summit is over 18 km (11 miles) high, and the summit caldera is about 63 km (39 miles) across. Also found in the Tharsis region are numerous other volcanos which, while smaller, are still giants in terms of Earth volcanoes. All of these are shield volcanoes and all are now extinct. The linear arrangement of many of these mountains has been interpreted by some researchers as a sign of plate tectonics on Mars. Two even larger volcanoes, Olympus Mons and Alba Mons lie to the northwest and north of Tharsis respectively.
caption: Tharsis volcanoes, colored using elevation data - white is high elevation, purple is low elevation.

name: Olympus Mons
description: This gigantic mountain is the largest volcano yet found in the solar system. The summit stands at an altitude of 21.1 km (13.1 miles), and is crowned by a complex caldera 72 x 91 km (45 x 57 miles) across. The base of the mountain is defined be a steep cliff up to 8 km tall and is 640 km across. However, vast aprons of lava flows extend for over 1,000 km (621 miles) from the summit towards the northwest. The volume of the mountain has been estimated to be an incredible 2,400,000 cubic km. Olympus Mons is a shield volcano, build of innumerable flows of quite fluid lava. Some of the flows on the northwest flank may possibly be as young as 2 million years. Olympus Mons formed off the northwest edge of the older Tharsis volcanic plateau.
caption: Olympus Mons is the largest volcano found in the solar system.

name: Alba Mons
description: Though Olympus Mons is the tallest and most massive of the Martian volcanoes, one other volcano has a greater diameter. Alba Mons has a base 1015 x 1150 km (631 x 715 miles) across. The summit stands 6.8 km (4.2 miles) high and is topped by a caldera 106 x 138 km (66 x 86 miles) across. It is a shield volcano, apparently built of fluid lava flows and ash deposits. Its very broad, low profile makes it harder to distinguish than many of the other volcanoes in the area. Located on the northern edge of Tharsis, Alba Mons exhibits very ancient lava flows. Its flanks are notable for vast systems of great parallel faults, such as those seen in the Ceraunius Fossae.
caption: Alba Mons, a shield volcano built of fluid lava flows and ash deposits.

name: Kasei Valles
description: The Kasei Valles form one of the more spectacular systems of outflow channels on the surface of Mars. Roughly 1,800 km (1,118 miles) long and 480 km (300 miles) wide, the system of huge canyons was likely carved by one or more gigantic floods. Kasei drained a vast area running north from the vicinity of Valles Marineris and along the eastern edge of Tharsis. Kasei Valles emptied into Chryse Planitia from the west.
caption: Kasei Valles was likely carved by one or more gigantic floods.

name: Shalbatana Vallis
description: Shalbatana Vallis is a very prominent outflow channel that runs prominently northeast from the crater Orson Welles, covering a distance of about 680 km (422 miles) before emptying into Chryse Chaos. It was carved by one or more catastrophic floods of water. Shalbatana Vallis is noted for clear signs of shorelines and delta deposits.
caption: The outflow channel Shalbatana Vallis was carved by one or more floods of water.

name: Ares Vallis
description: One of the great outflow channels on Mars, Ares Vallis drained the area of Margaritifer Chaos into Chryse Planitia through a spectacular 1,700 km (1,056 miles) long channel. NASA’s Pathfinder mission with the Sojourner rover landed in the region where Ares Vallis emptied into Chryse Planitia, in an area rich in deposits streamlined by the flow of water.
caption: Ares Vallis is one of the great outflow channels on Mars.

name: Elysium Volcanic Region
description: The second-largest of Mars’ volcanic regions (after Tharsis), Elysium is the site for three of Mars' great shield volcanoes. Hecates Tholus has a base 177 x 187 km (110 x 116 miles) across. Its summit stands 4.8 km (3 miles) high and is crowned by a caldera 13 km (8 miles) across. Elysium Mons is 375 km (233 miles) across, has a summit 14.1 km (8.8 miles) high, and a caldera 14 km (8.7 miles) across. Albor Tholus has a base 157 x 164 km (98 x 102 miles) across, has a summit 4.1 km (2.5 miles) high, and a caldera 36 km (22 miles) across. Elysium is also marked by a number of systems of large faults including the Cerberus Fossae, Elysium Fossae, and Hephaestus Fossae.
caption: Three of Mars' great shield volcanoes located in the Elysium Volcanic Region.
